question.text:
Which of the following integers has a multiplicative inverse modulo $42?$

  1. $12$
  2. $25$
  3. $37$
question.explanation:
An integer $a$ has a multiplicative inverse modulo $n$ if and only if $a$ and $n$ are coprime, i.e., $\textrm{gcd}(a,n)=1.$

With this in mind, let's examine the given options.

  • $12$ does not have a multiplicative inverse modulo $42$ since $\textrm{gcd}(12,42)=6\neq1. \:\:{\color{red}\times}$

  • $25$ has a multiplicative inverse modulo $42$ since $\textrm{gcd}(25,42)=1. \:\:{\color{darkgreen}\checkmark}$

  • $37$ has a multiplicative inverse modulo $42$ since $\textrm{gcd}(37,42)=1. \:\:{\color{darkgreen}\checkmark}$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

example.title: Determining the Existence of a Multiplicative Inverse

question.text: Use trial and error to compute the following residue.
question.explanation:
The multiplicative inverse of $3$ modulo $8,$ denoted $3^{-1},$ is the number $x$ such that

\[ 3 \cdot x \equiv 1 \quad (\textrm{mod}\:8). \]

Note that since $\text{gcd}(3, 8) = 1,$ an inverse element exists and is unique up to congruence modulo $8.$

Since the modulus $n=8$ is small, we can find the inverse $x$ by computing exponents of $3$ (modulo $8$) until we get a result of $1\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} 3^2 &\equiv 3 \cdot 3 \equiv 9 \equiv 1\cdot 8 + 1\equiv 1 && (\textrm{mod}\:8) \end{align*}

So, $3 \cdot 3 \equiv 1 \, (\textrm{mod} \:8).$ Therefore, the multiplicative inverse of $3$ modulo $8$ is $\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{3}.$

question.text: Use trial and error to compute the following residue.
question.explanation:
The multiplicative inverse of $7$ modulo $12,$ denoted $7^{-1},$ is the number $x$ such that

\[ 7 \cdot x \equiv 1 \quad (\textrm{mod}\:12). \]

Note that since $\text{gcd}(7,12) = 1,$ an inverse element exists and is unique up to congruence modulo $12.$

Since the modulus $n=12$ is small, we can find the inverse $x$ by computing exponents of $7$ (modulo $12$) until we get a result of $1\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} 7^2 &\equiv 7\cdot 7 \equiv 49 \equiv 4\cdot 12 + 1\equiv 1 && (\textrm{mod}\:12) \end{align*}

So, $7 \cdot 7 \equiv 1 \, (\textrm{mod} \:12).$ Therefore, the multiplicative inverse of $7$ modulo $12$ is $\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{7}.$

question.text: Fill in the blanks to make the following reasoning true.
question.explanation:
First of all, notice that $\textrm{gcd}(85,211)=\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{1}.$ So, the multiplicative inverse of $85$ modulo $211$ exists.

The multiplicative inverse of $85$ modulo $211$ is the number $x$ such that

\[ 85 \cdot x \equiv 1 \quad (\textrm{mod}\:211). \]

To find the value of $x,$ we will use the extended Euclidean algorithm. First, we apply the forward reduction:

\begin{align*} \begin{matrix} \color{red}211& = & \color{red}85\cdot 2 & + & \color{red}41 \\ & \swarrow & & \swarrow & \\ \color{blue}85& = & \color{blue}41 \cdot 2 & + & \color{blue}3 \\ & \swarrow & & \swarrow & \\ \color{magenta}41 & = & \color{magenta}3 \cdot 13 & + & \color{black}2 \\ & \swarrow & & \swarrow & \\ \color{black}3 & = & \color{black}2 \cdot 1& + & \color{black}1 \\ \end{matrix} \end{align*}

Solving for the rightmost terms in the equations above, we get

\begin{align*} \color{red}41 &= \color{red} 211 - 85 \cdot 2 \\[5pt] \color{blue}3 &= \color{blue} 85- 41\cdot 2 \\[5pt] \color{magenta}2 &= \color{magenta} 41- 3\cdot 13 \\[5pt] 1 &= 3-2. \end{align*}

Then, we back-substitute:

\begin{align*} 1 &= 3-{\color{magenta}2} \\[5pt] &= 3-{\color{magenta}(41-3\cdot 13)} \\[5pt] &= {\color{blue}3}\cdot 14 -41 \\[5pt] &= {\color{blue}(85-41\cdot 2)}\cdot 14 - 41 \\[5pt] &= 85\cdot 14 -{\color{red}41} \cdot 29 \\[5pt] &= 85\cdot 14 - {\color{red}(211 - 85\cdot 2)} \cdot 29 \\[5pt] &= 85 \cdot 72 - 211 \cdot 29 \\[5pt] &= 85\cdot \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{72} + 211\cdot (\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{-29}) \\[5pt] \end{align*}

We can write this result modulo $211,$ as follows:

\begin{align*} 85\cdot 72 + 211\cdot (-29)& \equiv 1 && (\text{mod}\:211) \\[5pt] 85\cdot 72 & \equiv 1 && (\text{mod}\:211) \\[5pt] \end{align*}

So, we have $85\cdot 72\equiv 1 \: (\textrm{mod}\:211),$ which means that $85^{-1} \: \textrm{mod} \: 211 =\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{72}.$

question.text: Fill in the blanks to make the following reasoning true.
question.explanation:
First of all, notice that $\textrm{gcd}(69,82)=\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{1}.$ So, the multiplicative inverse of $69$ modulo $82$ exists.

The multiplicative inverse of $69$ modulo $82$ is the number $x$ such that \[ 69 \cdot x \equiv 1 \quad (\textrm{mod}\:82). \]

To find the value of $x,$ we will use the extended Euclidean algorithm. First, we apply the forward reduction: \begin{align*} \begin{matrix} \color{red}82 & = & \color{red}69\cdot 1 & + & \color{red}13 \\ & \swarrow & & \swarrow & \\ \color{blue}69& = & \color{blue}13 \cdot 5 & + & \color{blue}4 \\ & \swarrow & & \swarrow & \\ \color{black}13 & = & \color{black}4 \cdot 3 & + & \color{black}1 \\ \end{matrix} \end{align*}

Solving for the rightmost terms in the equations above, we get \begin{align*} \color{red}13 &= \color{red} 82 - 69 \\[5pt] \color{blue}4 &= \color{blue} 69 - 13\cdot 5 \\[5pt] 1 &= 13 - 4\cdot 3. \end{align*}

Then, we back-substitute: \begin{align*} 1 &= 13-{\color{blue}4}\cdot 3 \\[5pt] &= 13-{\color{blue}(69-13\cdot 5)}\cdot 3 \\[5pt] &= 13-69\cdot 3 + 13\cdot 15 \\[5pt] &= {\color{red}13} \cdot 16 - 69\cdot 3 \\[5pt] &= {\color{red}(82-69)} \cdot 16 - 69\cdot 3 \\[5pt] &= 82 \cdot 16 - 69\cdot 16 - 69\cdot 3 \\[5pt] &= 82 \cdot 16 - 69\cdot 19 \\[5pt] &= 69\cdot (\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{-19}) + 82 \cdot \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{16} \\[5pt] \end{align*}

We can write this result modulo $82,$ as follows: \begin{align*} 69 \cdot (-19) + 82 \cdot 16& \equiv 1 && (\text{mod}\:82) \\[5pt] 69 \cdot (-19) & \equiv 1 && (\text{mod}\:82) \\[5pt] 69\cdot (82-19) & \equiv 1 && (\text{mod}\:82) \\[5pt] 69\cdot 63 & \equiv 1 && (\text{mod}\:82) \\[5pt] \end{align*}

So, we have $69\cdot 63\equiv 1 \: (\textrm{mod}\:82),$ which means that $69^{-1} \: \textrm{mod} \: 82=\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{63}.$
